paragraphs: The importance of the Union from a commercial point of view is one of those matters on which there is the least room for a difference of opinion, and it has in fact won the widest agreement among men who know anything of the subject. This holds as much for our dealings with foreign countries as for our dealings with one another.

There is reason to suppose that the adventurous spirit that marks the commercial character of America has already caused uneasiness among several of the maritime powers of Europe. They seem to fear that we will interfere too much in the carrying trade, which supports their shipping and is the foundation of their naval strength. Those among them that have colonies in America look ahead with painful anxiety to what this country is capable of becoming. They foresee the dangers that may threaten their American dominions from the neighborhood of States that have every disposition, and would have every means, needed to create a powerful navy. Impressions of this kind will naturally point to a policy of fostering divisions among us and of depriving us, as far as possible, of an ACTIVE COMMERCE in our own ships. This would serve a threefold purpose: preventing our interference in their shipping, monopolizing the profits of our trade, and clipping the wings on which we might rise to a dangerous greatness. If prudence did not forbid going into detail, it would not be difficult to trace, by facts, the workings of this policy to the cabinets of ministers.

If we remain united, we can counteract a policy so unfriendly to our prosperity in a variety of ways. By prohibitory regulations extending at the same time throughout the States, we can oblige foreign countries to bid against each other for the privilege of our markets. This assertion will not seem fanciful to those who can appreciate how important the markets of three million people are to any manufacturing nation. Those people are increasing at a rapid rate, are for the most part devoted exclusively to agriculture, and are likely from local circumstances to remain so. Nor will it seem fanciful to those who can appreciate the immense difference it would make to the trade and shipping of such a nation whether its products and returns travel to and from America directly in its own ships or indirectly in the ships of another country. Suppose, for instance, that we had a government in America capable of shutting Great Britain (with whom we have at present no treaty of commerce) out of all our ports. What would the probable effect of this step be on her politics? Would it not enable us to negotiate, with the fairest prospect of success, for commercial privileges of the most valuable and extensive kind in the dominions of that kingdom? When these questions have been asked on other occasions, the answer given has been plausible but neither solid nor satisfactory. It has been said that prohibitions on our part would produce no change in the system of Britain, because she could carry on her trade with us through the Dutch, who would be her immediate customers and paymasters for the articles needed to supply our markets. But would not her shipping be materially injured by losing the important advantage of being her own carrier in that trade? Would not the main part of its profits be taken by the Dutch as compensation for their services and risk? Would not the mere matter of freight cause a considerable deduction? Would not so roundabout a trade make it easier for other nations to compete, by raising the price of British goods in our markets and by transferring to other hands the management of this important branch of British commerce?

Careful consideration of the matters these questions raise will justify the belief that the real disadvantages to Britain from such a state of things would produce a relaxation in her present system. They would do so in combination with the leanings of a great part of the nation in favor of the American trade and with the importunities of the West India islands. She would then admit us to privileges in the markets of those islands and elsewhere from which our trade would draw the most substantial benefits. Such a point gained from the British government, which could not be expected without an equivalent in exemptions and immunities in our markets, would be likely to have a corresponding effect on the conduct of other nations, who would not be inclined to see themselves altogether supplanted in our trade.

A further resource for influencing the conduct of European nations toward us in this respect would arise from the establishment of a federal navy. There can be no doubt that if the Union continued under an effective government, we would have it in our power, before very long, to create a navy that, even if it could not rival those of the great maritime powers, would at least carry respectable weight if thrown into the scale of either of two contending parties. This would be especially true of operations in the West Indies. A few ships of the line, sent at the right moment to reinforce either side, would often be enough to decide the fate of a campaign on whose outcome interests of the greatest magnitude depended. Our position in this respect is a most commanding one. And if we add to this the usefulness of supplies from this country in carrying on military operations in the West Indies, it is easy to see that so favorable a situation would enable us to bargain with great advantage for commercial privileges. A price would be set not only on our friendship but on our neutrality. By steady adherence to the Union we may hope, before long, to become the arbiter of Europe in America, and to be able to tip the balance of European rivalries in this part of the world as our interest may dictate.

But in the opposite of this desirable situation, we shall find that the rivalries of the separate parts would make them checks upon each other and would defeat all the tempting advantages that nature has kindly placed within our reach. In a state so insignificant, our commerce would be a prey to the wanton meddling of all nations at war with each other. Having nothing to fear from us, they would with little scruple or remorse supply their needs by plundering our property whenever it fell in their way. The rights of neutrality will be respected only when they are defended by adequate power. A nation made contemptible by its weakness forfeits even the privilege of being neutral.

Under a vigorous national government, the natural strength and resources of the country, directed toward a common interest, would defeat every combination of European jealousy to restrain our growth. This situation would even remove the motive for such combinations, since success would be impossible. Active commerce, extensive shipping and a flourishing navy would then be the offspring of moral and physical necessity. We could defy the little arts of the little politicians to control or alter the irresistible and unchangeable course of nature.

But in a state of disunion these combinations might exist and might work with success. The maritime nations, taking advantage of our universal weakness, would be able to dictate the conditions of our political existence. They have a common interest in being our carriers, and a still greater interest in preventing our becoming theirs. They would therefore in all probability combine to obstruct our shipping in a way that would in effect destroy it and confine us to a PASSIVE COMMERCE. We should then be forced to content ourselves with the first price of our goods, and to see the profits of our trade snatched from us to enrich our enemies and persecutors. That unequaled spirit of enterprise that distinguishes the character of American merchants and navigators, and that is in itself an inexhaustible mine of national wealth, would be stifled and lost. Poverty and disgrace would overspread a country that, with wisdom, might make herself the admiration and envy of the world.

There are rights of great importance to the trade of America that are rights of the Union. I allude to the fisheries, to the navigation of the Western lakes, and to that of the Mississippi. The dissolution of the Confederacy would open delicate questions about the future existence of these rights, which the interest of the more powerful parties would hardly fail to settle to our disadvantage. The disposition of Spain with regard to the Mississippi needs no comment. France and Britain share the fisheries with us and regard them as of the utmost importance to their shipping. They, of course, would hardly remain indifferent for long to that decided mastery in this valuable branch of trade that experience has shown us to possess, and by which we are able to undersell those nations in their own markets. What is more natural than that they should be disposed to bar from the field such dangerous competitors?

This branch of trade ought not to be regarded as a benefit to one part only. All the seafaring States may share in it advantageously, in different degrees, and with a greater extension of commercial capital would not be unlikely to do so. As a nursery of seamen it now is, or when time shall have brought the principles of navigation in the individual States closer together will become, a resource for all. For the establishment of a navy it must be indispensable.

To this great national object, a NAVY, union will contribute in various ways. Every institution will grow and flourish in proportion to the quantity and extent of the means gathered for its formation and support. A navy of the United States, because it would draw on the resources of all, is an object far less remote than a navy of any single State or partial confederacy, which would draw on the resources of only one part. It happens, indeed, that different portions of confederated America each possess some particular advantage for this essential establishment. The more southern States furnish certain kinds of naval stores, tar, pitch and turpentine, in greater abundance. Their wood for building ships is also more solid and lasting. The difference in the lifespan of the ships that would make up the navy, if built chiefly of Southern wood, would be of signal importance for either naval strength or national economy. Some of the Southern and of the Middle States yield iron in greater plenty and of better quality. Seamen must chiefly be drawn from the Northern hive. The need for naval protection of foreign or maritime commerce requires no particular explanation, any more than the way that kind of commerce contributes to the prosperity of a navy.

Unrestrained trade among the States themselves will advance the commerce of each by an exchange of their respective products, not only to supply reciprocal needs at home but for export to foreign markets. The veins of commerce in every part will be replenished, and will gain additional motion and vigor from a free circulation of the goods of every part. Commercial enterprise will have much greater scope from the diversity in the products of different States. When the staple of one fails because of a bad harvest or an unproductive crop, it can call to its aid the staple of another. The variety of products for export, no less than their value, contributes to the activity of foreign commerce. It can be carried on on much better terms with a large number of materials of a given value than with a small number of materials of the same value, because of the competition of trade and the fluctuations of markets. Particular articles may be in great demand at certain times and unsalable at others. But if there is a variety of articles, it can scarcely happen that they will all be in the latter condition at one time, and for this reason the merchant's operations would be less liable to any considerable obstruction or stagnation. The speculative trader will see the force of these observations at once, and will acknowledge that the aggregate balance of the commerce of the United States would stand a fair chance of being much more favorable than that of the thirteen States without union or with partial unions.

It may perhaps be replied that, whether the States are united or disunited, there would still be an intimate trade between them that would serve the same ends. But this trade would be fettered, interrupted and narrowed by a multiplicity of causes, which in the course of these papers have been amply detailed. A unity of commercial interests, as well as political, can result only from a unity of government.

There are other points of view, of a striking and animating kind, from which this subject might be considered. But they would lead us too far into the regions of the future, and would involve topics not suitable for a newspaper discussion. I shall observe briefly that our situation invites us, and our interests prompt us, to aim at ascendancy in the system of American affairs. The world may be divided into four parts, politically as well as geographically, each having a distinct set of interests. Unhappily for the other three, Europe, by her arms and her negotiations, by force and by fraud, has in different degrees extended her dominion over them all. Africa, Asia and America have in turn felt her domination. The superiority she has long maintained has tempted her to plume herself as the Mistress of the World and to consider the rest of mankind as created for her benefit. Men admired as profound philosophers have in direct terms attributed a physical superiority to her inhabitants, and have gravely asserted that all animals, and with them the human species, degenerate in America, and that even dogs cease to bark after breathing our atmosphere for a while.(1) Facts have too long supported these arrogant pretensions of the Europeans. It belongs to us to vindicate the honor of the human race, and to teach that presuming brother, moderation. Union will enable us to do it. Disunion will add another victim to his triumphs. Let Americans disdain to be the instruments of European greatness! Let the thirteen States, bound together in a strict and indissoluble Union, join in erecting one great American system, superior to the control of all transatlantic force or influence, and able to dictate the terms of the connection between the old and the new world!
